title: American Presbyterians in the Revolutionary Era
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
series: American Presbyterians in the Revolutionary Era

outline.title: The Theological Foundation: Proverbs 11:11
subpoints: The moral and spiritual condition of a people determines the fate of their nation.
Blessing and ruin are not random but flow from the character of the people in relation to God.
The revolution was driven by convictions of conscience and the sovereignty of God over earthly power.

outline.title: The Perception of the Revolution in England
subpoints: Horace Walpole’s remark that America 'ran off with the Presbyterian parson.'
John Witherspoon as the primary figure associated with the Presbyterian character of the revolution.
Witherspoon’s role as the only ordained clergyman to sign the Declaration of Independence.

outline.title: The Scots-Irish Presbyterian Heritage
subpoints: Migration route from Scotland to Ulster (Ireland) and then to America.
Persecution under James I and the desire for religious liberty.
Settlement in the frontier regions of Pennsylvania, Virginia, and the Carolinas.

outline.title: Establishment of American Presbyterianism
subpoints: Francis McKim’s role in planting churches and establishing the Philadelphia Presbytery in 1706.
The Philadelphia Presbytery as the first confessional denomination with a national existence in America.
The precedent set by McKim’s release from arrest for preaching without a license.

outline.title: Revival and the Path to Independence
subpoints: The impact of the First Great Awakening on the revolutionary generation.
Support for revivalist preachers like George Whitefield and Jonathan Edwards.
The shift from a focus on individual rights to a focus on duty to God and the community.

summary:
This sermon explores the significant role of American Presbyterians, particularly those of Scots-Irish descent, in the founding of the United States and the Revolutionary Era. Pastor Lyro begins by establishing a theological framework using Proverbs 11:11, arguing that the moral and spiritual integrity of a people directly influences the destiny of their nation. He highlights the perception in England that the revolution was driven by Presbyterian convictions, citing the famous remark by Horace Walpole and the pivotal role of John Witherspoon, the only ordained minister to sign the Declaration of Independence.

The session traces the historical migration of Presbyterians from Scotland to Ulster and finally to the American frontier, noting their pursuit of religious liberty and their settlement in the middle and southern colonies. Key figures such as Francis McKim are discussed, emphasizing the establishment of the Philadelphia Presbytery as the first nationally organized confessional body in America. The sermon concludes by connecting the spiritual fervor of the First Great Awakening to the revolutionary spirit, suggesting that the era was defined not merely by political strategy but by a deep-seated sense of duty to God and a commitment to the principles of conscience and sovereignty that shaped the new nation.
